## Claims

### Authorship
- **[genuineness questioned]** Ephesians "presents itself unambiguously as a letter from Paul the apostle," but authenticity "has frequently been questioned, beginning in the late eighteenth century (Hoehner 2002: 6)." (Thielman reporting history of debate)
- **[pseudonymity context]** Fictional letters in a famous person's name were "reasonably common in Greco-Roman antiquity" and "particularly popular from the third century BC to the first century AD." Thielman surveys a continuum: innocent fiction (Epistles of Anacharsis), forgery-to-deceive ("Plato's" Ep. 12, per Donelson 1986), and in-between (Socratic epistles).
- **[Christian pseudepigraphy]** Deceptive Christian pseudonymity existed (Marcionite letters to Laodiceans/Alexandrians "forged in Paul's name," Muratorian Canon 63–65; Pseudo-Clementine Homilies; Apostolic Constitutions). Donelson (1986:17): "Christian pseudepigraphy found its main impetus in doctrinal disputes, the endless argument between orthodoxy and heresy."
- **[ancient forgery NOT tolerated]** Thielman argues (with Metzger 1972, Wilder 2004, J. Marshall 2008) that Greco-Roman society was NOT more tolerant of forgery — exile at Athens, amputation under Claudius, Galen's and Jerome's complaints. "There is no reason to think that early Christians were any more tolerant of forged documents than anyone else."
- **[Thielman's own core argument against pseudonymity]** The "noble lie" (Plato Rep.; adopted by Clement of Alexandria, Strom. 7.9) motivated Christian forgery only in doctrinal crisis — but **"Ephesians is not a polemical document"** (contra Smith 1977, Merz 2000); "there is no theological battle raging behind the text that might justify the extreme measure of a 'noble lie'" against the author's "otherwise high standards of honesty (4:15, 24–25; 5:9; 6:14)."
- **[anomaly argument]** "if Ephesians is pseudonymous, it is something of an anomaly among Christian pseudonymous letters" — it urges truthful speech (4:25) yet would lie about its own author "without any clear moral justification." Paul's first-person self-portrait as a suffering apostle near martyrdom (3:1, 13; 4:1; 6:19–20) does not read as innocent fiction.
- **[Thielman's conclusion]** "The text makes sense as an authentic letter from Paul to Christians in Ephesus, written at the end of a lengthy period of imprisonment and thus after nearly all of his undisputed correspondence (i.e., Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon)."
- **[list of undisputed letters]** Thielman's operative list of undisputed Paulines given explicitly (above); he treats 2 Thessalonians as Pauline for argument's sake (line 143).

### Literary Character / Style
- **[universal agreement it is difficult]** Chrysostom called it ὑπέρογκος (hyperonkos, "sublime"/"difficult"); Origen (via Jerome) said Paul "heaped up more obscure ideas and mysteries unknown to the ages in this epistle than in all the others" (Heine 2002:78); Erasmus linked it to 2 Pet. 3:16 ("things difficult to understand").
- **[three unusual style features]** (1) High number of very long sentences — "Ephesians has 2,422 words in the NA27 edition… 64 sentences" vs Galatians' 2,230 words in 102 sentences; six especially long sentences: 1:3–14, 15–23; 2:1–7; 3:1–7; 4:11–16; 6:14–20. (2) Grammatical/lexical ambiguities affecting meaning (many examples: 1:17, 1:23, 2:2, 2:14, 2:21, 3:17, 6:24). (3) Highly redundant (e.g. "the good pleasure of his will" 1:5; "the counsel of his will" 1:11).
- **[missing argumentative feel]** "Rhetorical questions, if-then clauses, and syllogisms are virtually absent" (cf. van Roon 1974).
- **[non-Pauline diction]** Uses non-Pauline words for Pauline concepts ("the devil" for "Satan," "the heavenly places" for "heaven") or Pauline words in unprecedented ways ("fullness" applied to the church) — cited by pseudonymity advocates (De Wette, Holtzmann, Moffatt, Mitton, Lincoln).
- **[Thielman: Paul could write this way]** Two evidences: (1) the undisputed Paul wrote in varied styles (1 Cor. 13; Phil. 2:6–11; Rom. 16:25–27); (2) long/broken syntax appears elsewhere in the corpus (Eph. 1:3–14 ≈ 2 Thess. 1:3–12; cf. 1 Cor. 1:4–8; Phil. 1:3–7; Rom. 5:12–18). Imprisonment + dictation with little chance to revise "accounts for this unusual element."

### Relationship to Colossians
- **[closest style match]** "The style of Colossians comes closest to that of Ephesians" — long sentences, redundant genitive-strung phrases, one rhetorical question each (Col 2:20 / Eph 4:9), little lively argumentation.
- **[verbal overlap data]** Mitton (1951): "26.5 percent of the wording of Colossians appears in Ephesians"; yet apart from the Tychicus passage "the most protracted verbatim correspondence does not exceed seven words, and on only three occasions exceeds five." Mitton concludes the author's "mind was saturated with the contents of Colossians." Tychicus commendation shares 32 words (Eph 6:21–22 / Col 4:7–9), including a 10-word and a 19-word consecutive stretch.
- **[Mitton's pseudonymity argument]** Verbal convergence + conceptual divergence at the same points → the two can't be simultaneous → different authors. Mitton's divergence examples (line 65–115): Col 2:19 head of cosmos vs Eph 4:15–16 head of church; ἀποκαταλλάσσω reconcile-to-God (Col 1:20,22) vs reconcile-Jew/Gentile (Eph 2:16); revelation τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ (Col 1:26) vs τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις… (Eph 3:5); μυστήριον = Christ in Col vs varied in Eph; οἰκονομία = Paul's assignment (Col 1:25) vs providential dispensation (Eph 1:9–10; 3:9); πλήρωμα (Christ/God in Col vs Christ/church & Christian maturity in Eph).
- **[Thielman rebuts Mitton]** "Mitton's analysis (1951) is largely unconvincing." Points 1–2 rest on "improbable exegesis" (Col 2:19 body = church, not cosmos, per Col 1:18,24; Eph 2:16 reconciles both to God). The μυστήριον/οἰκονομία/πλήρωμα terms are too infrequent in Colossians and the undisputed letters to fix a "semitechnical" meaning. Only the Col 1:26 / Eph 3:5 comparison is "more convincing," but is equally explicable as same-author expansion (Bockmuehl 1990). Thielman: the stylistic-closeness/conceptual-difference argument convinces "only to those who are already convinced on other grounds that Ephesians is pseudonymous."
- **[most think Eph used Col]** "Usually, the author of Ephesians is thought to have used Colossians (e.g., Mitton 1951:68–74)."

### Recipients & the "in Ephesus" (ἐν Ἐφέσῳ) textual problem
- **[most general letter]** "Ephesians is the most general letter within the Pauline corpus." Only associate named is Tychicus; no greetings, no thanks, no travel plans, limited knowledge of readers (heard of their faith 1:15; assumes they know his commission 3:2 and received Jesus' teaching 4:21). Puzzling if it went to Ephesus, where Paul spent 2–3 years (Acts 19:10; 20:31).
- **[the crux]** The two words ἐν Ἐφέσῳ in 1:1 are "the only indication in the text… that it was intended for Ephesus, and those words are missing in some of the letter's oldest manuscripts." "One of the most difficult textual problems in the New Testament."
- **[manuscript data]** Earliest witness 𝔓46 (3rd-c. Alexandrian) omits the place name, reads τοῖς ἁγίοις οὖσιν καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (no article). Other Alexandrians (א, B, 1739, 6, 424c) omit ἐν Ἐφέσῳ but add article τοῖς before οὖσι[ν]. Marcion may have titled it "To the Laodiceans" (Tertullian, Marc. 5.17.1). Origen (AD 233–44) and Basil the Great (363–65) both worked from texts lacking the place name; both puzzled over the grammar of τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσι; Basil said the "old copies" had this reading.
- **[problems with the no-place-name reading]** (1) "almost insuperable grammatical difficulties" — τοῖς οὖσιν needs a place name (as in Phil 1:1; 2 Cor 1:1; Rom 1:7); makes "no sense" without it, so the lectio-difficilior rule doesn't apply. (2) Witnesses omitting it are almost all Alexandrian (limited geographical spread; Hoehner 2002:146). Emendation theories (circular letter with blank space — Lightfoot, Zuntz, Luz; scribal insertion — Best 1997a; original Hierapolis/Laodicea address — van Roon, Lincoln) each face objections (esp. why the καί survives).
- **[the majority reading]** τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — supported by A, 33, 81, 1175, 1881, 104 (Alexandrian affinities), correctors of א and B, Western D F G (D omits article like 𝔓46), Byzantine K L P, plus versions and fathers of wide geographical spread. "This geographical diversity… weighs heavily in favor of treating this reading as original."
- **[Thielman's verdict]** "on balance the arguments in favor of reading 'in Ephesus' seem to outweigh those against it." Even mss omitting it have subscriptions reading "to the Ephesians" (Metzger 1994:543); Origen and Basil believed Paul wrote to Ephesus. Parallel scribal universalizing: "in Rome" omitted at Rom 1:7 in Codex G; Tertullian (Marc 5.17): "of what consequence are the titles, since in writing to a certain church the apostle did in fact write to all?" Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact (native Greek speakers) found the phrase unproblematic.
- **[the real difficulty]** The deepest problem for "in Ephesus" is the letter's impersonal tone toward a church Paul served ~3 years (1:15 "heard"; 3:2, 4:21 "if… you have heard/were taught"; Abbott 1897:78: "No preacher addressing those whom he himself had taught would ordinarily express himself in this way"). Thielman resolves this by the historical circumstances (7+ year absence), not by rejecting the place name.

### Date & Setting in Paul's Career
- **[Thielman's dating]** Paul wrote Ephesians "near the end of his two-year imprisonment in Rome and at roughly the same time as Colossians and Philemon, in AD 62." Chained to a soldier but free to receive visitors (incl. a dictation secretary); sent all three letters with Tychicus.
- **[Ephesian ministry dates]** Paul spent 2–3 years in Ephesus, "probably the years AD 52–54 (Schnabel 2004:1220)," great success esp. among Gentiles; only Jewish Christians attested before his arrival (Trebilco 2004:125–27).
- **[imprisonment identification]** Ephesians fits the long confinement of Acts (Caesarea 2 yrs, Malta, then 2 yrs Rome "from spring 60 to sometime in 62," Acts 28:30–31) under "light… military custody" (Rapske 1994:182) — "unhindered" (Acts 28:31), enough freedom for dictation. Prayer request (6:19–20 "enchained ambassador") suggests awaiting a judicial hearing.
- **[Tychicus as courier]** Tychicus fits the ancient letter-courier profile (Richards 2004; Head 2009); from Asia (Acts 20:4), name mostly attested at Rome; appears in Col 4:7–9 (32 shared words). Thielman prefers the explanation that Paul dictated the two letters in close succession and had the secretary reuse the commendation — an "almost exact precedent" in two genuine Ignatius letters (Phld. 11.2; Smyrn. 12.1).
- **[Colossians fills the blanks]** Companions present (Epaphras, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus-Justus, Luke, Demas); Philemon shows Paul hoped for release and travel east — coheres with light custody near the end of imprisonment.

### Circumstances / Occasion
- **[range of theories rejected]** From "no specific circumstances" (Robinson 1904 — a supreme non-controversial exposition of "the unity of mankind in Christ") to hyper-specific reconstructions (Kirby 1968 — an Ephesian's liturgical composition to fill a Corinthian request). Thielman: highly specific proposals are speculative and reach no consensus; but the "no circumstances" view also fails because the letter voices specific concerns (prayers 1:18–23, 3:17–19; unity/faithfulness 4:1–16; moral warnings 4:17–19, 5:3–18; encouragement re: Paul's suffering 3:13).
- **[Thielman's reconstruction]** Readers exhibited "a certain weariness in the readers' commitment to the gospel," leading to disunity and moral compromise (cf. Lincoln 1990). Two decisive cultural factors: (1) the religious culture of first-century Ephesus, (2) the Judaism–Christianity relationship.
- **[Ephesus religious milieu]** Reputation for magic and worship of Ephesian Artemis (= Diana). Jerome (relying on Origen): Paul speaks more of "obscure ideas and mysteries" and of demons here because the environment was "obsessed with demons and magic" and idolatry ("multi-breasted Diana"). "Rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (3:10; 2:2; 6:12) confirmed by studies of the city (Strelan, Schnabel, Trebilco, Brinks); Arnold (1989) reads "power" in the letter against this background.
- **[imperial cult]** Ephesus was "an especially important center of the imperial cult" (Friesen 2001:128). Temple (AD 11–13) to Artemis + Augustus + Tiberius + the demos. Key point: the ~9 BC Asian calendar reform centered time on Augustus's birthday; the koinon decree called him "a savior" (σωτήρ) and "god" (θεός), his birthday "the beginning of good tidings [euangelia] to the world" (OGIS 458). Friesen: "Augustus would make sense of time"; imperial cult claimed the household's rule was "eternal." **Thielman's exegetical payoff:** Eph 1:9–10 (God administering the times, summing up all things in Christ), 1:21–22 (victory over every authority, all things "under his feet"), 2:7 (eternal kindness) would read as counter-claims that "Christ, not Augustus… is the Lord of time and that only his reign is eternal." (attributed to Thielman's reading, grounded in Friesen)
- **[Judaism–Christianity factor]** Old approach (Calvin — anti-Judaizer aim; F.C. Baur 2003 — 2nd-c. pseudonymous gnostic/Montanist synthesis of Jewish+Gentile Christianity; Schlier, Käsemann — gnostic mythology reminding Gentiles of Jewish roots). Thielman: the gnostic-mythology reading "has fallen precipitously from favor" (rests on texts postdating Ephesians by centuries). But the Judaism–Christianity concern "is well founded… rests firmly on 2:11–22 (cf. 3:6)."
- **[Lincoln & MacDonald]** Both place the letter post-Paul (Lincoln: AD 80–90 disorientation after Paul's death, fading parousia hope, cultural accommodation, household code lowers tension; MacDonald: Domitian's reign 81–96, Jewish-tax [fiscus Judaicus] pressures, legitimation of new leadership structures tied to apostles/prophets). Thielman finds "this picture… largely convincing."
- **[Thielman's key divergence — authentic dating]** He does NOT need a post-death date: "If Paul wrote the letter around AD 62… then he had been confined… for nearly five years and absent from Ephesus for over seven years. This is enough time for the conditions… to develop." Jewish-Christian/Gentile drift, house-church divergence (30–40 people per household, Trebilco), pre-Pauline groups (Apollos and the "brothers," Acts 18:24–28), and continuing tension with the Artemis/imperial/magic culture (Acts 19:23–34; Rev 2:3) all fit an AD 62 authentic letter.
- **[summary of occasion]** Ephesian house churches, mostly Gentile after 7+ years, had received little news of Paul, were discouraged by his suffering (3:13), disunified, tempted to assimilate. They needed reminding of (1) the power/grace of the one God, (2) the church's role in God's plan to unite the universe in Christ, (3) the resulting ethical responsibility.

### Structure & Outline
- **[mixed structure]** "a mixture of organization and spontaneity" — planned movement from praise/thanksgiving/intercession (1:3–14; 3:20–21; 1:15–23; 3:14–19) and description of God's blessings (2:1–3:13) to ethical admonition (4:1–6:20); yet extemporaneous (unclear section breaks at 2:1, 5:21; broken syntax; digressions 2:2–3, 14–18; 3:2–13).
- **[full 13-part outline]** (I) Prescript/greeting 1:1–2; (II) Blessing God 1:3–14; (III) Thanksgiving & intercession 1:15–23; (IV) From children of wrath to new creation 2:1–10; (V) From without-God to people-of-God 2:11–22; (VI) Paul's task & suffering for Gentiles 3:1–13; (VII) Prayer for inner strength 3:14–21; (VIII) Growth toward unity & maturity 4:1–16; (IX) Living as new humans 4:17–5:2; (X) Avoiding/transforming deeds of darkness 5:3–14; (XI) Wise household conduct 5:15–6:9 (wives/husbands, children/parents, slaves/masters); (XII) Standing against the devil 6:10–20; (XIII) Concluding commendation & prayer-wish 6:21–24.

### Commentary body — 1:1–2 (OVERFLOW, exegesis proper)
- **[1:1 apostleship]** Παῦλος ἀπόστολος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ. Paul asserts apostolic authority to address people "largely unknown" to him (parallel to Rom 1:1, Col 1:1, where apostleship wasn't disputed but readers were unknown — unlike Gal/1–2 Cor where it was challenged). Apostles = envoys sent on a mission; Paul is the type "called to preach the gospel to non-Jewish peoples" (Rom 1:5; 11:13; Gal 1:15–16), coupling "apostles and prophets" always in that order (2:20; 3:5; 4:11) at the church's foundation.
- **[1:1 recipients / grammar]** Thielman keeps ἐν Ἐφέσῳ. On the "two groups?" question (saints in Ephesus vs believers in Christ), he concludes a single group is meant: the division "is without precedent in Paul's other letters"; Paul calls all readers "saints" throughout (1:15,18; 3:8,18; 4:12; 5:3; 6:18), refuting the Jewish-Christians="saints"/Gentiles="believers" reading (Kümmel 1975). Grammatically the first τοῖς governs both ἁγίοις and πιστοῖς (Alford, Wallace 1996:282, Hoehner 2002:142); Chrysostom/Theodoret/Theophylact saw nothing unnatural.
- **[1:1 hagioi / pistoi]** ἅγιοι (saints) takes its sense from the OT (Exod 19:5–6; Lev 11:44–45): status given by God (5:26, hagiazō via the "cleansing bath of the gospel") to be lived out (1:4; 5:3). πιστοί here likely means "believers" (those who trusted the gospel, cf. 1:13 pisteusantes) rather than "faithful/loyal" (contra Origen, Lightfoot, Barth); with Lincoln, O'Brien, Hoehner. Both saints and believers ἐν Χριστῷ = existing "within the sphere… that Christ defines."
- **[1:1 Additional Note]** ἐν Ἐφέσῳ absent in 𝔓46, א, B; Origen and Basil lacked it; Basil noted "old copies" omitted it. Still likely original: wider geographical distribution, and omission "both violates Paul's normal practice of including a place name… and produces almost unintelligible Greek." Probably dropped in the Alexandrian tradition "in an effort to further universalize its already quite general contents."
- **[1:2 greeting]** "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" — identical to seven other letters (Rom, 1–2 Cor, Gal, Phil, 2 Thess, Philem). Fuses Greek χαίρειν (→ χάρις, charis) and Semitic šālôm (→ εἰρήνη, eirēnē) into a prayer-wish, not a mere greeting; may echo the priestly benediction (Num 6:23–26), functioning as an assertion of apostolic (priest-like) authority. Distinctively, grace/peace come also from "the Lord Jesus Christ," anticipating the letter's theme of Jesus as the means of God's grace (1:3–6; 2:5,7; 4:32) and peace (2:14–17; 6:23).

### Commentary body — structure of the 1:3–14 benediction (OVERFLOW)
- **[berakah form]** The benediction/berekah is the central Jewish prayer form (OT examples; Mishnah Berakot, first tractate of the first order); Jewish letters sometimes opened with benedictions (Tel Arad letters; Eupolemus). The 3 NT letters beginning with benedictions (2 Cor 1:3–4; Eph 1:3–14; 1 Pet 1:3–5) may follow this Jewish epistolary custom (Dahl 2000).
- **[unusual length]** Eph 1:3–14 is one sentence of **202 words**, vs 2 Cor 1:3–4 (44) and 1 Pet 1:3–5 (53); it sustains pure praise start to finish (root εὐλογ- three times in v.3: εὐλογητός/εὐλογήσας/εὐλογίᾳ) without straying into intercession/confession/admonition. Closest stylistic parallel: Qumran prayers, esp. 4Q434.
- **[hymn theory rejected]** The view that the passage is a pre-existing hymn/poem/liturgy (Innitzer, Lohmeyer; recent: Coutts, Fischer, Muddiman) "has now fallen from favor": (1) style and theology fit the whole letter seamlessly; (2) attempts to find poetic "period/cola" structure are subjective and inconsistent (Debrunner, van Roon).
- **[Thielman's own structural analysis]** Four semantic markers: (1) ἐν Χριστῷ phrases at section ends; (2) κατά/καθώς phrases + purpose clauses; (3) three active participles εὐλογήσας / προορίσας / γνωρίσας; (4) refrain "for the praise of his glory" (vv. 6, 12, 14), each closing a section featuring one Trinitarian person (Father vv.4–6, Christ vv.7–12, Spirit vv.13–14). No single marker accounts for the whole; small inconsistencies reveal "the extemporaneous nature of the passage."
- **[dictation thesis]** Best explained "if Paul dictated the passage extemporaneously but with some prior structure in mind" — like ancient use of the Eighteen Benedictions / Lord's Prayer as outlines rather than fixed wording.
- **[four-part division]** Using converging ἐν (Christ) + κατά markers, four parts, each internal boundary = an ἐν-phrase referring to Christ followed by ἐν ᾧ: A 1:3–6 (ends ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ); B 1:7–10 (ends ἐν αὐτῷ); C 1:11–12 (ends ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ); D 1:13–14 (switches to 2nd person, closes "for the praise of his glory," no κατά clause). Thematic flow: (A) God chose/predestined his people in Christ before creation for adoption; (B) redemption via Christ's death + revelation of the mystery of cosmic unification; (C) made heirs, summarizing A–B; (D) readers sealed with the Spirit as down-payment on future inheritance.
- **[christological focus]** Trinitarian in character (Innitzer, O'Brien, Hoehner) but "its main focus is Christ" (Fee 1994:665) — ten "in Christ" statements, six forming the structural hinges. Practical purpose: to remind discouraged readers (3:13) of all God has done for them in Christ.

## Named scholars/positions cited
- **Hoehner (2002)** — dating of authorship debate; grammar of 1:1 (single group); benediction structure.
- **Donelson (1986)** — pseudonymity typology; "noble lie" motive; pseudepigraphy driven by orthodoxy-vs-heresy disputes.
- **Metzger (1972, 1987, 1994)** — ancient intolerance of forgery; Muratorian Canon; subscription "to the Ephesians."
- **Wilder (2004)** — Socratic epistles; ancient attitudes to forgery.
- **Mitton (1951)** — Ephesians depends on Colossians; 26.5% verbal overlap; verbal-convergence/conceptual-divergence argument for pseudonymity (Thielman rebuts).
- **van Roon (1974)** — sentence lengths; Hierapolis/Laodicea address theory; hymn-structure critique.
- **Percy (1946)** — long sentences in the Pauline corpus.
- **Best (1997a, 1998)** — 1:1 text-critical theories; "two groups" grammar problem; benediction fits letter.
- **Lincoln (1990)** — pro-pseudonymity on style; post-Paul dating AD 80–90; occasion reconstruction.
- **Hoehner, Schnabel (2004), Trebilco (2004), Strelan (1996), Arnold (1989), Brinks (2009)** — Ephesian setting, Artemis, "powers."
- **Friesen (2001), Price (1984)** — imperial cult in Asia/Ephesus; calendar reform; eternal-rule ideology.
- **Calvin, F.C. Baur, Schlier, Käsemann, MacDonald (2000, 2004)** — Judaism–Christianity readings; MacDonald's Domitianic setting.
- **Rapske (1994), Richards (2004), Head (2009)** — imprisonment conditions; letter couriers.
- **Origen, Basil the Great, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Jerome, Erasmus** — patristic/reception voices on style, grammar, and the "in Ephesus" reading.
- **Bockmuehl (1990), Dahl (2000), Fee (1994), Caragounis (1977), Schnackenburg, Gnilka, Krämer, Innitzer, Lohmeyer** — benediction background/structure.

## Notable Greek terms with glosses
- ὑπέρογκος (hyperonkos) — "sublime"/"difficult" (Chrysostom's word for the letter).
- τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — "to the saints who are in Ephesus and believers, in Christ Jesus" (majority reading of 1:1).
- ἅγιοι (hagioi) — "saints" (OT-derived: God's set-apart people).
- πιστοί (pistoi) — "believers"/"faithful" (Thielman: "believers," those who trusted the gospel).
- ἐν Χριστῷ (en Christō) — "in Christ" (sphere of existence; structural hinge of 1:3–14).
- ἀποκαταλλάσσω (apokatallassō) — "reconcile" (Col 1:20,22; Eph 2:16).
- μυστήριον (mystērion) — "mystery" (varies: Christ / cosmic reunification / Jew-Gentile unity / "symbol" 5:32).
- οἰκονομία (oikonomia) — "administration/assignment"/"providential dispensation" (1:9–10; 3:9).
- πλήρωμα (plērōma) — "fullness" (Christ-God; Christ-church; Christian maturity).
- χάρις (charis) / εἰρήνη (eirēnē) — "grace" / "peace" (1:2 greeting; grace ↔ χαίρειν, peace ↔ šālôm).
- εὐλογητός / εὐλογήσας / εὐλογία (eulogētos/eulogēsas/eulogia) — "blessed / who has blessed / blessing" (v.3 wordplay).
- εὐαγγέλιον / εὐανγέλιον (euangelion) — "gospel"/"good tidings" (contested between Christ and the Augustus imperial-cult proclamation).
- σωτήρ (sōtēr) / θεός (theos) — "savior" / "god" (imperial-cult titles for Augustus, OGIS 458).
- προορίσας (proorisas) — "having predestined" (1:5); γνωρίσας (gnōrisas) — "having made known" (1:9).
- εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ (eis epainon tēs doxēs autou) — "for the praise of his glory" (refrain, vv. 6, 12, 14).
